title: Grammar Fundamentals for Clear Communication

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a subject and its verb as dance partners who must step together. One person dancing alone takes the solo step: 'The nurse checks.' A whole group takes the group step: 'The nurses check.' Person matters too, which is why 'I am' and 'she is' use different forms of the same verb. Other nouns hanging around the sentence do not get a vote; only the actual subject decides the verb's step.

### Question 2

An independent clause is like a person who can live alone: it has someone doing something (the subject) and the doing itself (a finite verb). 'The patient rested.' That is a whole sentence. Put 'because' in front and it suddenly needs a roommate: 'Because the patient rested...' leaves the reader waiting. Note that the subject and verb are still there; the subordinating word is what makes the clause dependent rather than independent.

### Question 3

A pronoun works like a shortcut arrow pointing backward. When a reader hits 'his,' the mind flips back to find who is meant and lands on 'patient.' The word the arrow lands on is the antecedent, from Latin roots meaning 'going before.' The trouble starts when the arrow points at nothing, or at two possible people, as in 'The nurse told the patient that she was late' -- the reader cannot tell who 'she' is.

### Question 4

A comma is a speed bump, not a stop sign. Two complete sentences meeting each other need something stronger: a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a joining word like 'and.' When only the speed bump is used, the sentences slide into each other, and that slide is a comma splice. The related error with no mark at all is a fused or run-on sentence; both are fixed by choosing a bigger traffic signal.

### Question 5

An opening word group like 'While charting the assessment' never names its own doer, so English assigns it the subject of the clause that follows the comma. Here that subject is 'the call light,' so the sentence claims a plastic device was doing paperwork. The modifier is left dangling with nothing sensible to attach to. The fix is either to put the real actor right after the comma or to write the doer into the opening group itself.

### Question 6

Active voice puts the doer in the driver's seat: 'The nurse gave the medication.' Passive moves the doer to the back seat or leaves them out entirely: 'The medication was given.' Neither is against the rules. Passive helps when nobody knows who acted, or when the thing done matters more than the person who did it. But when accountability is the point, put the driver back behind the wheel so the reader knows exactly who acted.

### Question 7

Cover the words between the subject and the verb with your thumb and reread: 'Each ___ responsible.' The ear immediately supplies 'is.' The phrase 'of the nurses' is scenery along the way, and scenery does not get to control the verb. 'Each' means one at a time, so it stays singular no matter how large the group it selects from. The same test works for 'either,' 'neither,' and 'one of.'

### Question 8

Words like 'however' sound like joining words, but they cannot actually hold two sentences together; they are commentary, not glue. The semicolon does the holding, and 'however' rides just after it with a comma trailing: stable; however, dizzy. Use only a comma and the two sentences collapse into a splice. Put the semicolon after 'however' and the commentary gets stranded away from the clause it was meant to introduce.

### Question 9

A relative clause attaches to whatever noun it sits beside. In the original it sits beside 'patient,' so the reader first hears that the patient was printed in Spanish and then has to back up and reinterpret. English lets you say 'gave the patient the instructions' just as easily as 'gave the instructions to the patient,' so reordering puts 'instructions' where the clause can reach it. Changing the seating chart usually beats adding words.

### Question 10

Here is the test that never fails: read the sentence substituting 'it is.' If it still makes sense, write 'it's,' where the apostrophe stands in for the missing letter in 'is.' If 'it is' sounds wrong, you want plain 'its,' the ownership word, which takes no apostrophe for the same reason 'his' and 'hers' do not. The form 'its'' with a trailing apostrophe is never correct in any sentence.

### Question 11

Test a list by checking whether every item can finish the opening words on its own: 'emphasized reading...,' 'emphasized attending...,' 'emphasized that students should submit...' The first two are -ing phrases and the third is a full clause, so the pattern breaks partway through and the reader has to reset. Convert the odd item to match, giving 'submitting drafts early,' and all three slot in identically. That matching is parallelism, and it is what makes lists scannable.

### Question 12

Commas here mark the difference between a condition and an aside. With no commas, the clause is doing filtering work: only those particular students may enter. Add commas and the clause becomes a side note, as though everyone already qualifies and you are simply noting it. Two small marks quietly shift the rule from 'some may enter' to 'all may enter,' which is why the restrictive versus nonrestrictive distinction matters in policies and instructions.
